nodeData.note: A complex group is a family of companies where a subsidiary owns its own subsidiary, or where the parent owns a company both directly and through another subsidiary. This topic also covers what happens when the parent buys more shares, or sells some, over time.

children.note: Start here: who owns whom, and why the group still reports as one business.

children.topic: One family, one set of accounts
children.note: Group accounts show the parent and everything it controls as if they were a single business (a single economic entity). Inside trading is cancelled out.

manas.q: What does "single economic entity" mean in group accounts?

children.note: A company is consolidated when the parent controls it: power over the key activities, exposure to its returns, and the ability to use that power to affect those returns.

manas.q: Under IFRS 10, what three things make up control?

children.note: You already know goodwill, non-controlling interest (NCI), cancelling intra-group items and associates under IAS 28. Complex groups use the same tools, just with more layers.
The parent owns a subsidiary, and that subsidiary owns another company. The bottom company is a sub-subsidiary of the parent.

manas.q: What is a vertical (sub-subsidiary) group?

children.note: The parent owns some shares in a company directly AND more shares through one of its subsidiaries. Drawn on paper, the lines make a D shape.

manas.q: What is a mixed or D-shaped group?

children.note: Groups change: a parent may buy more shares in stages (step acquisition), or sell some or all of its shares (disposal). Each change has its own accounting rule.
Investors in the parent need to see the whole group. Wrong percentages or dates give the wrong goodwill, wrong NCI and a wrong profit figure.
Four IFRS standards work together for this topic. Learn what each one does in plain words.
Tells you when to consolidate (when you have control) and how to treat changes in ownership, including losing control.

manas.q: Which standard sets the control test and the rules on losing control?

children.note: Tells you how to account for the day you gain control: measure what you paid, the NCI and the net assets at fair value, and work out goodwill.

manas.q: Which standard covers goodwill on the date control is gained?

children.note: IAS 28 Investments in Associates and Joint Ventures covers significant influence (usually 20%–50%) and the equity method. Needed when an interest is an associate before or after a change.
IFRS 12 Disclosure of Interests in Other Entities asks the group to explain in the notes its subsidiaries, associates, NCI that matter, and the effect of changes in ownership.

manas.q: What does IFRS 12 deal with?

children.note: Smaller Kenyan groups may use IFRS for SMEs, which has simpler group rules. CPA Advanced exams use full IFRS.
How to handle a chain: H owns S, and S owns T.

children.topic: Is T a subsidiary of H?
children.note: Yes, if H controls S and S controls T. Control passes down the chain, even if H's effective share of T is below 50%.

manas.q: Can a sub-subsidiary be consolidated when the effective interest is under 50%?

children.note: Multiply the percentages down the chain. If H owns 80% of S and S owns 60% of T, H effectively owns 0.8 × 0.6 = 48% of T.

manas.q: How do you calculate the effective interest in a sub-subsidiary?

children.topic: NCI in T: direct plus indirect
children.note: NCI in T is everything H does not effectively own: 100% − 48% = 52%. That is 40% held by outsiders directly in T plus 12% held through S's own NCI (20% × 60%).

manas.q: How is NCI in a sub-subsidiary worked out?

children.note: Use the later of two dates: when H got control of S, or when S got control of T. T joins the group only once both links exist.

manas.q: What date is used to consolidate a sub-subsidiary?

children.topic: Cost of T from the group view
children.note: S paid for T, but H only owns 80% of S. So in T's goodwill working use only H's share of what S paid (80% of S's cost).

manas.q: What cost of investment is used in the sub-subsidiary goodwill working?

children.note: The other 20% of S's cost of T belongs to S's NCI. Deduct it from NCI so the investment is not counted twice.
Group retained earnings take H's 80% of S's post-acquisition profit and 48% of T's. The rest goes to NCI.
The parent holds the same company in two ways: directly and through a subsidiary.
H owns 60% of S and 25% of T. S owns 40% of T. H holds T both directly (25%) and through S.
H controls 25% of T's votes itself and 40% through S, which it controls: 65% in total. So T is a subsidiary.

manas.q: In a mixed group, how do you test whether the parent controls the bottom company?

children.note: Direct 25% plus indirect 60% × 40% = 24%, so H's effective interest in T is 49%. NCI in T is 51%.

manas.q: How is the effective interest in a mixed group calculated?

children.note: Cost of T for the group = H's direct cost plus H's 60% share of S's cost. Each purchase may have a different date and fair value, so check dates carefully.
Use voting control to decide IF T is consolidated. Use the effective interest to SPLIT T's profit between the group and NCI.
Buying shares in stages until you gain control.
The investor already holds some shares (often as an associate or a simple investment), then buys more and gains control. IFRS 3 calls this control achieved in stages.

manas.q: What is a step acquisition?

children.note: On the control date, revalue the shares you already held to fair value. Any gain or loss goes to profit or loss.

manas.q: In a step acquisition, what happens to the previously held interest?

children.topic: Rule 2: goodwill at control date only
children.note: Goodwill = what you paid now + fair value of the old holding + NCI − fair value of net assets, all measured on the day control is gained.

manas.q: What is the goodwill formula in a step acquisition?

children.note: While it was an associate, the old holding was equity-accounted under IAS 28. That carrying amount is what you compare with fair value.
Buying more shares in a company you already control is NOT a step acquisition. No new goodwill and no gain; it is a deal between owners in equity.
Selling shares: did the parent lose control or keep it?
This one question decides everything. Lost control: a gain or loss in profit or loss. Kept control: an equity transaction with no gain in profit or loss.

manas.q: What is the key question when a parent sells shares in a subsidiary?

children.note: Group gain = proceeds + fair value of any shares kept + NCI carrying amount − (net assets + goodwill) at disposal date.

manas.q: How is the group gain on losing control calculated?

children.note: If the parent keeps, say, 30%, that holding is remeasured to fair value and becomes an associate (IAS 28) or an investment from then on.
In H's own books the gain is simply proceeds minus the cost of the shares sold. The group gain is different because it uses net assets and goodwill.

manas.q: How is the gain on disposal worked out in the parent's own accounts?

children.note: Selling a small slice while still in control just moves value between owners. NCI goes up, and the difference to cash goes to equity, not profit or loss.

manas.q: How is a partial disposal that keeps control accounted for?

children.note: Buying more shares from the NCI is the mirror image: NCI goes down, cash goes out, and any difference is taken to equity.
In the year of a change, consolidate the subsidiary's income only up to the date control is lost (or from the date gained). Split profits by date.
Real numbers in KES millions (KES m). Every figure ties.
Nairobi-based H bought 80% of S on 1 Jan 2023 for KES 400m. S had bought 60% of T on 1 Jan 2022 for KES 200m. NCI is measured at its share of net assets.
H in S 80%, NCI in S 20%. H effective in T = 80% × 60% = 48%. NCI in T = 52%.
S controlled T from 2022, but H controlled S only from 1 Jan 2023. So T is consolidated from 1 Jan 2023.
Fair value of S's net assets: KES 420m (this includes its KES 200m investment in T). Fair value of T's net assets: KES 300m.

children.topic: Example 1: goodwill in S and T
children.note: Goodwill is worked at 1 Jan 2023 for both companies.
Cost 400 + NCI (20% × 420 = 84) − net assets 420 = KES 64m.
Group cost (80% × 200 = 160) + NCI (52% × 300 = 156) − net assets 300 = KES 16m.
64 + 16 = KES 80m on the group balance sheet.
At 31 Dec 2025 S has made KES 50m and T KES 100m since 1 Jan 2023.
84 − indirect holding adjustment (20% × 200 = 40) + 20% × 50 = KES 54m.
Net assets: H 700 (excl. investment) + S 270 (excl. investment) + T 400 + goodwill 80 = 1,450. Equity: share capital 500 + RE 688 + NCI 262 = 1,450.
H held 30% of A (an associate) carried at KES 90m. On 1 Jul 2025 H bought another 50% for KES 250m. The old 30% was worth KES 140m that day; A's net assets were KES 380m.
Fair value 140 − carrying amount 90 = KES 50m gain in profit or loss. Dr Investment in A 50 / Cr Profit or loss 50.
Paid 250 + old holding 140 + NCI (20% × 380 = 76) − net assets 380 = KES 86m.
H bought 80% of S for KES 300m when S's net assets were 300; NCI 60, goodwill 60. Later, with net assets of 400 and NCI of 80 (60 + 20% × 100), H sells the whole 80% for KES 450m.
Proceeds 450 + NCI 80 − (net assets 400 + goodwill 60) = KES 70m gain in group profit or loss.
Proceeds 450 − cost 300 = KES 150m. Different from the group's 70 because the group already counted S's profits and goodwill.
Sell 50% for 300; the kept 30% is worth 170. Gain = 300 + 170 + 80 − (400 + 60) = KES 90m. The 30% becomes an associate at 170.
H owns 90% of S and sells 10% for KES 70m. S's net assets are KES 500m; NCI is measured at share of net assets.
NCI rises by 10% × 500 = KES 50m.
Dr Cash 70 / Cr NCI 50 / Cr Equity (parent's reserves) 20. Nothing goes to profit or loss.
H owns 60% of S; NCI (40%) stands at KES 200m. H buys another 20% from NCI for KES 130m.
NCI falls by 20/40 × 200 = 100. Dr NCI 100 / Dr Equity 30 / Cr Cash 130. No new goodwill.
Where marks are usually lost.
For T in a chain, the group's share is the effective 48%, not the 60% that S holds. NCI in T is 52%, not 40%.
A sub-subsidiary bought before the parent bought S is consolidated from the date H got S, using T's fair values on that later date.
In T's goodwill use only 80% of S's cost. Forgetting this overstates goodwill and NCI.
Do not test control with the effective percentage. A 48% effective holding can still be a subsidiary because control flows down the chain.
A partial sale that keeps control never creates a gain in profit or loss. It goes to equity.
In a step acquisition, the old holding must be taken to fair value first, with the gain or loss in profit or loss.
Try each one, then open the steps.
H owns 75% of S and S owns 70% of T. What are H's effective interest and the NCI in T?
Effective interest = 75% × 70% = 52.5%.
NCI in T = 100% − 52.5% = 47.5%. T is still a subsidiary because control passes down the chain.
H gains control by buying more. The old 20% is now worth KES 60m. What is the gain?
60 − 45 = KES 15m gain in profit or loss; the 60 is used in the goodwill working.
Proceeds KES 90m; S's net assets KES 400m; NCI at share of net assets.
Still 65%, so control is kept: equity transaction.
NCI up by 15% × 400 = 60. Dr Cash 90 / Cr NCI 60 / Cr Equity 30.
Proceeds 200, net assets 150, goodwill 20, NCI 30. What is the group gain?
200 + 30 − (150 + 20) = KES 60m gain in group profit or loss.

nodeData.note: How to record deals done in another currency, and how to bring a foreign subsidiary into the group accounts. The rules come from IAS 21 The Effects of Changes in Foreign Exchange Rates. This topic builds on Complex groups and the CA23 group accounts topics.

children.topic: What it is and why it matters
children.note: Kenyan businesses buy, sell and invest across borders. Exchange rates move every day, so the shilling value of a foreign deal keeps changing. IAS 21 tells you which rate to use and where the gain or loss goes.
The price of one currency in another, for example KES per US dollar. All rates in this map are made up for teaching, so each is marked 'illustrative rate'.

manas.q: What is an exchange rate?

children.note: The gain or loss that appears when the same foreign amount is turned into shillings at two different rates.

manas.q: What is an exchange difference under IAS 21?

children.note: Job 1: record a single company's foreign deals (transactions). Job 2: turn a whole foreign subsidiary's accounts into the group's currency (translation).

manas.q: What are the two main areas IAS 21 covers?

children.note: Listed companies and most groups use full IFRS, so IAS 21 applies. Smaller entities using IFRS for SMEs follow a similar section on foreign currency.
Before any translation, decide the company's own working currency and the currency the accounts are shown in.
The currency of the main economic setting where the business earns and spends its cash. A Nairobi shop selling and paying in shillings has KES as functional currency.

manas.q: What is functional currency?

children.note: Look first at which currency mainly sets selling prices and which currency mainly pays wages, materials and other costs. Then look at how it raises loans and keeps cash.

manas.q: What are the main clues for choosing a functional currency?

children.note: The currency the financial statements are shown in. A company may choose any presentation currency, for example a Kenyan group reporting in USD for investors.

manas.q: What is presentation currency?

children.note: Any currency other than the entity's functional currency. For a Mombasa importer with KES functional currency, USD is a foreign currency.
Only when the underlying business facts change. The change is applied from that date forward, not backwards.

manas.q: How is a change in functional currency applied?

children.note: Rules for a single company that buys or sells in a foreign currency.

children.topic: Day one: use the spot rate
children.note: Record the deal in your functional currency at the exchange rate on the day it happens (the spot rate). An average rate for a week or month is fine if rates do not move much.

manas.q: At what rate is a foreign currency transaction first recorded?

children.topic: Monetary items: money owed or held
children.note: Items that are cash or will be received or paid as a fixed number of currency units: cash, receivables, payables, loans.

manas.q: What is a monetary item?

children.note: Items with no right to a fixed amount of money: inventory, property, plant and equipment, prepaid rent, goodwill.

manas.q: Give examples of non-monetary items.

children.note: At the reporting date, restate monetary items at the closing rate. The difference goes to profit or loss.

manas.q: How are foreign monetary items treated at the year end?

children.note: Items at historical cost stay at the rate on the day they were bought. Items carried at fair value use the rate on the day fair value was measured.

manas.q: Which rate is used for non-monetary items?

children.note: How the exchange difference arises depends on whether the bill is paid before the year end.
Paid before year end. One exchange difference: the gap between the recorded amount and the cash actually paid. It goes to profit or loss.

manas.q: How is an exchange difference on a settled transaction treated?

children.note: Still owed at year end. Retranslate at the closing rate and take the difference to profit or loss now; a second difference arises when it is finally paid.

manas.q: How is an unsettled foreign payable treated at year end?

children.topic: When a currency cannot be exchanged
children.note: 2023 amendments (Lack of Exchangeability, for periods from 1 January 2025): if you cannot swap a currency in a normal market, estimate the rate an orderly deal would use, and explain it in the notes.

manas.q: What do the 2023 Lack of Exchangeability amendments to IAS 21 require?

children.note: To consolidate a subsidiary that keeps its books in another currency, first translate its statements into the group's presentation currency. This is the closing rate method.
Every asset and liability in the subsidiary's balance sheet uses the rate at the reporting date.

manas.q: Which rate translates a foreign subsidiary's assets and liabilities?

children.note: Strictly each item uses its own transaction-date rate. An average rate for the year is accepted as a close approximation if rates did not swing a lot.

manas.q: Which rate translates a foreign subsidiary's income and expenses?

children.note: Equity at acquisition (share capital and pre-acquisition reserves) stays at the rate on the acquisition date. Post-acquisition profits build up at the rates used each year.
Because different lines use different rates, a difference appears. It goes to other comprehensive income and builds up in a separate equity reserve.

manas.q: Where do translation differences on a foreign subsidiary go?

children.note: Goodwill and fair value adjustments on acquiring a foreign operation are treated as its assets. Keep them in the foreign currency and retranslate at the closing rate each year.

manas.q: How is goodwill on a foreign subsidiary treated under IAS 21?

children.note: If the group owns less than 100%, the non-controlling interest takes its share of the translation difference, just like profit.
On disposal, the translation reserve built up for that subsidiary moves from equity to profit or loss (reclassification) as part of the gain or loss on disposal.

manas.q: What happens to the translation reserve when a foreign subsidiary is sold?

children.topic: Loans that are part of the investment
children.note: If the parent lends to the subsidiary with no plan to be repaid, the loan is part of the net investment. In the group accounts its exchange differences go to OCI, not profit or loss.
Kenyan examples with made-up rates. Every rate here is an illustrative rate, not a real market rate.
A Mombasa importer (functional currency KES) buys goods for USD 10,000 on credit from a US supplier on 1 October. Year end is 31 December; payment is made on 15 February.
Illustrative rate KES 130/USD. USD 10,000 x 130 = KES 1,300,000. Dr Inventory KES 1,300,000 / Cr Trade payables KES 1,300,000.
Illustrative rate KES 132/USD. Payable now KES 1,320,000, up KES 20,000. Dr Exchange loss (P&L) KES 20,000 / Cr Trade payables KES 20,000. Inventory stays at KES 1,300,000.
Illustrative rate KES 128/USD. Cash paid KES 1,280,000. Dr Trade payables KES 1,320,000 / Cr Cash KES 1,280,000 / Cr Exchange gain (P&L) KES 40,000. Debits = credits = KES 1,320,000.
Illustrative rate KES 131/USD: cash KES 1,310,000. Dr Trade payables KES 1,300,000, Dr Exchange loss KES 10,000 / Cr Cash KES 1,310,000. Settled, so nothing to retranslate at year end.
Nairobi Holdings bought 100% of Kampala Ltd on 1 January when its net assets were share capital UGX 300m. Kampala keeps books in UGX. Rates are UGX per KES 1, all illustrative.
Illustrative rates, UGX per KES 1: 25 at acquisition (1 Jan), 27.5 average for the year, 30 at 31 December. More UGX per shilling means the UGX got weaker.
PPE 240m + inventory 90m + cash 96m = 426m, less payables 60m = net assets 366m. Equity: share capital 300m + profit for the year 66m = 366m.
At illustrative closing rate 30: PPE KES 8.0m, inventory 3.0m, cash 3.2m = 14.2m; payables 2.0m; net assets KES 12.2m.
Share capital at illustrative historical rate 25: UGX 300m / 25 = KES 12.0m. Profit at illustrative average rate 27.5: UGX 66m / 27.5 = KES 2.4m.
Net assets KES 12.2m less share capital 12.0m less profit 2.4m = translation reserve KES -2.2m (a loss, to OCI). Equity 12.0 + 2.4 - 2.2 = KES 12.2m, so it balances.
Opening net assets: 300/30 - 300/25 = 10.0 - 12.0 = -2.0m. Profit: 66/30 - 66/27.5 = 2.2 - 2.4 = -0.2m. Total KES -2.2m, matching the balancing figure.
Nairobi paid KES 13.2m. At illustrative rate 25: KES 13.2m x 25 = UGX 330m, less net assets UGX 300m = goodwill UGX 30m.
UGX 30m / 25 (illustrative rate) = KES 1.2m.
UGX 30m / 30 (illustrative closing rate) = KES 1.0m. Fall of KES 0.2m: Dr OCI (translation reserve) 0.2m / Cr Goodwill 0.2m.
KES 2.2m on net assets + KES 0.2m on goodwill = KES 2.4m in OCI. If Kampala is later sold, this KES 2.4m moves to profit or loss.
Places where students most often lose marks.
Only monetary items go to the closing rate in a single company. Inventory and equipment bought abroad stay at the historical rate.
For a foreign subsidiary, translation differences go to OCI, not profit or loss, until the subsidiary is sold.

children.topic: Goodwill left at the old rate
children.note: Goodwill on a foreign subsidiary must be retranslated at the closing rate every year; the change goes to the translation reserve.
Check how the rate is quoted. KES per USD: multiply USD by the rate. UGX per KES: divide UGX by the rate. Ask: should the shilling number be bigger or smaller?
Functional currency is a fact found from the business; presentation currency is a choice. Do not swap them.
When the group owns less than 100%, split the translation difference between the parent and the non-controlling interest.
Try each question, then open the bubbles for the steps. All rates are illustrative.
A Thika flower exporter (KES) sells to a UK buyer for GBP 20,000 on credit. Illustrative rate on sale KES 170/GBP; at year end KES 165/GBP. Show the entries.
20,000 x 170 = KES 3,400,000. Dr Trade receivables KES 3,400,000 / Cr Revenue KES 3,400,000.
20,000 x 165 = KES 3,300,000. Receivable falls KES 100,000. Dr Exchange loss (P&L) KES 100,000 / Cr Trade receivables KES 100,000.
A Ugandan subsidiary earns UGX 54m profit. Illustrative average rate UGX 27 per KES 1. What is the profit in KES?
Income and expenses use the average rate: UGX 54m / 27 = KES 2.0m.
A Kenyan subsidiary sells crude oil priced in USD, and most of its costs and loans are in USD. What is its functional currency?
USD. Sales prices and most costs are set in USD, so that is the main economic environment, even though the company is in Kenya.
A group sells a foreign subsidiary with a cumulative translation loss of KES 2.4m in equity. Where does it go?
Reclassify it from equity to profit or loss as part of the gain or loss on disposal: Dr P&L (disposal) KES 2.4m / Cr Translation reserve KES 2.4m.

maps.title: CA32 · 3. Sustainability reporting (IFRS S1 and S2)

nodeData.note: Sustainability reporting tells investors and lenders how issues like climate change could change a business's cash, its access to loans and its future. IFRS S1 sets the general rules and IFRS S2 covers climate. Kenya is phasing these standards in, starting with big public interest entities.

children.topic: What it is and why it matters
children.note: Start here: what these reports are, who reads them and why accountants now prepare them.

Financial statements show past results. Sustainability reporting adds forward-looking facts about risks and chances (opportunities) such as drought, new laws or clean energy that can change future cash flows.

children.topic: Who reads it: investors and lenders
children.note: The main users (primary users) are present and possible investors, lenders and other creditors deciding whether to give the business money.

manas.q: Who are the primary users of IFRS sustainability disclosures?

children.topic: Who sets the rules: the ISSB
children.note: The International Sustainability Standards Board (ISSB) sits under the IFRS Foundation, the same family that oversees the IASB and IFRS Accounting Standards.

manas.q: Which body issues IFRS S1 and IFRS S2?

children.note: IFRS S1 gives the general rules for any sustainability topic. IFRS S2 adds the detailed rules for climate. Both were issued in June 2023.
The question is how a sustainability matter affects the business's prospects, not just how the business affects the world. Impacts matter when they feed back into cash, finance or risk.
The numbers must link to the financial statements, use the same group and period, and be reliable. That is accounting work: data, controls, judgement and review.
IFRS S1 General Requirements for Disclosure of Sustainability-related Financial Information. Effective for annual periods beginning on or after 1 January 2024.
Tell users about the sustainability risks and opportunities that could reasonably be expected to affect the entity's cash flows, access to finance or cost of capital.

manas.q: What is the objective of IFRS S1?

children.note: Risks and opportunities are judged over the short, medium and long term. The entity explains what each time frame means for it.
Information is material if leaving it out, getting it wrong or hiding it could reasonably be expected to influence the decisions of primary users. Judge it for your own business.

manas.q: When is sustainability information material under IFRS S1?

children.topic: Same reporting entity as the accounts
children.note: The sustainability report covers the same entity as the financial statements. For a group, that is the parent and its subsidiaries, exactly as consolidated in topic 1.

manas.q: Which entity does an IFRS S1 report cover?

children.note: Report for the same period as the financial statements and publish at the same time, usually inside the annual report.

manas.q: When must IFRS S1 disclosures be reported?

children.note: Show how the sustainability facts link to each other and to the financial statements, for example using the same assumptions as impairment tests.

manas.q: What does "connected information" mean in IFRS S1?

children.note: Consider risks in your suppliers, customers and the places you operate, not just your own factory or office.
For topics with no specific IFRS standard, S1 points the entity to the SASB Standards and other guidance to find what to report.
An entity may say it complies with IFRS Sustainability Disclosure Standards only if it meets all their requirements.
A business may apply S1 early only if it also applies S2 at the same time.

manas.q: Can IFRS S1 be applied early on its own?

children.note: Both S1 and S2 organise disclosures under the same four headings, taken from the TCFD approach.
Who in the business watches these risks: the board, a committee, management, and how often they discuss them.

manas.q: Name the four core content areas of IFRS S1 and S2.

children.note: What the risks and opportunities are, how they affect the business model, plans and finances now and in future.
How the business finds, judges, ranks and watches these risks, and whether this sits inside its normal risk process.
The numbers used to track performance, the targets set and progress towards them.
"Good Sustainability Reports Matter": Governance, Strategy, Risk management, Metrics and targets.
IFRS S2 Climate-related Disclosures, issued June 2023 and effective for periods beginning on or after 1 January 2024. It builds on the TCFD recommendations.
Damage from the climate itself. Sudden events (acute) like floods; slow changes (chronic) like rising heat or less rain affecting a Naivasha flower farm.

manas.q: What are climate-related physical risks?

children.note: Risks from the move to a low-carbon economy: new laws, carbon taxes, new technology, customers changing tastes, damage to reputation.

manas.q: What are climate-related transition risks?

children.note: Chances to gain: solar power, energy saving, green products, green bonds or loans at better rates.
The business tests how its strategy would hold up under different climate futures (scenario analysis) and explains the result.

manas.q: What is climate scenario analysis used for under IFRS S2?

children.note: If the business has a plan to cut emissions or adapt, it explains the plan, its targets and how it will pay for it.
Numbers every business gives: greenhouse gas emissions, assets and activities exposed to climate risks and opportunities, climate spending, internal carbon prices and climate-linked pay.

manas.q: Give three cross-industry metrics required by IFRS S2.

children.note: Extra metrics for each industry, drawn from the SASB Standards, e.g. different measures for banks, farms or airlines.

manas.q: Where do the industry-based requirements in IFRS S2 come from?

children.note: The ISSB issued Amendments to Greenhouse Gas Emissions Disclosures in December 2025 to make some emission rules simpler and cheaper to apply.
S2 asks for emissions in tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (tCO2e), measured using the Greenhouse Gas Protocol and split into three scopes.
Direct emissions from sources the business owns or controls, such as its own diesel generators, boilers and delivery lorries.

manas.q: What are Scope 1 emissions?

children.note: Indirect emissions from producing the electricity, heat or steam the business buys, e.g. power bought from the national grid.

manas.q: What are Scope 2 emissions?

children.note: All other indirect emissions, upstream and downstream: suppliers' production, transport by others, staff commuting, customers using your products.

manas.q: What are Scope 3 emissions?

children.note: It depends on other people's data, so it uses estimates. It is often the biggest scope, so explain the method and the uncertainty.
The GHG Protocol lets a group count emissions by control (100% of what it controls) or by equity share (its % of ownership). State which one you used.

manas.q: What two ways can a group set its emissions boundary?

children.note: Emissions divided by a business size measure, e.g. tCO2e per KES million of revenue, so firms of different sizes can be compared.
ICPAK announced on 6 September 2023 that Kenya would adopt IFRS S1 and S2, and published its roadmap in November 2024.
From 1 January 2024 any organisation may apply S1 and S2 voluntarily.
Mandatory for public interest entities (PIEs) for periods beginning on or after 1 January 2027. Check ICPAK's definition of a PIE.

manas.q: When do IFRS S1 and S2 become mandatory for Kenyan public interest entities?

children.note: Mandatory for large entities that are not PIEs for periods beginning on or after 1 January 2028.
Mandatory for small and medium-sized non-PIEs for periods beginning on or after 1 January 2029.

children.note: Government organisations come later; ICPAK will set the date.

nodeData.note: A reconstruction is a plan to rescue a company that is losing money: shareholders and lenders agree to give something up today so the business can survive and pay them more later. You learn the law, the bookkeeping, and how to judge if a plan is fair and will work.

children.note: Start here: why a struggling company reorganises instead of closing.

children.topic: A rescue plan for a sick company
children.note: The company has big past losses, too much debt or no cash. A reconstruction rearranges its capital and debts so it can carry on trading.

manas.q: What is a capital reconstruction?

children.note: In a liquidation, assets are sold cheaply and most people get little. If the business can make profits again, a rescue usually gives everyone more.
Years of losses, a negative retained earnings balance, unpaid preference dividends, an overdraft at its limit, suppliers chasing payment and loan terms being broken.
Making the share capital smaller on paper, for example cutting each KES 10 share to KES 2. No cash leaves the company; it is used to wipe out losses.

manas.q: What is a capital reduction?

children.note: The same company carries on. Its own shares and debts are changed and losses written off inside its own books.

manas.q: What is an internal reconstruction?

children.note: A new company is formed to take over the old company's business. The old company is wound up and its members and creditors get shares or debentures in the new one.

manas.q: What is an external reconstruction?

children.note: Topic 4 builds on complex groups (group reorganisations) and foreign currency (rescues often involve foreign loans that grew when the shilling fell).
Kenyan company law gives the procedures; accountants put the numbers to them. Check the current Acts on Kenya Law before advising a client.
A company may reduce its share capital by a special resolution (75% of votes). This must be backed either by a solvency statement from directors (private companies) or by court confirmation.

manas.q: In Kenya, how can a company reduce its share capital?

children.note: Directors state that the company can pay its debts now and over the next year. Signing a false one is an offence, so directors must check the cash flow forecasts.

manas.q: What is a solvency statement?

children.note: The court checks that creditors are protected. Creditors may object, and the court can ask the company to pay or secure them first.
A compromise with a class of members or creditors. Each class votes separately, a large majority by value must agree, and the court must approve it. It then binds everyone in that class.

manas.q: What is a scheme of arrangement?

children.note: An administrator (a licensed insolvency practitioner) takes over to try to rescue the company as a going concern. A moratorium stops creditors suing while the plan is worked out.

manas.q: What is administration under the Insolvency Act 2015?

children.note: Directors propose a deal to creditors, such as paying 60 cents per shilling over three years. A supervisor oversees it. Once creditors approve, it binds them all.

manas.q: What is a company voluntary arrangement (CVA)?

children.note: The supermarket chain ran short of cash from 2016 and an administrator was appointed. The rescue failed; branches were sold and creditors voted to liquidate in January 2020.
One temporary account collects all the gains and losses of the scheme.
Also called a capital reduction or reorganisation account. Credit it with amounts given up by shareholders and lenders; debit it with losses and asset write-downs.

manas.q: What goes on each side of the reconstruction account?

children.note: Share capital cancelled, preference capital reduced, debt forgiven by lenders. These are the 'funds' that pay for the clean-up.
Accumulated losses, goodwill and other intangibles with no value, assets written down to fair value, and expenses of the scheme.
If credits exceed debits, the extra goes to a capital reserve. If debits are higher, the scheme is too small and must take more sacrifices.

manas.q: What happens to a credit balance left on the reconstruction account?

children.note: Write assets down to realistic values: obsolete stock, bad debts, old machines. Otherwise the 'after' balance sheet still overstates the company.
Unpaid dividends are not a liability until declared, so they are not in the books. If the scheme gives shares for them, Dr Reconstruction / Cr Share capital.

manas.q: How are preference dividend arrears treated in a scheme?

children.note: Most schemes need fresh cash, often a rights issue to existing shareholders. Dr Cash / Cr Share capital (and share premium if above par).
Who gets paid first if the company dies decides who should give up most in a rescue.
Costs of the liquidation, preferential creditors (such as staff wages), floating charge holders, unsecured creditors, then preference shareholders, then ordinary shareholders last.

manas.q: What is the order of payment in a liquidation?

children.note: Paid from the sale of their security. They are safest, so they should give up least. Any shortfall becomes an unsecured debt.
Suppliers and an unsecured bank overdraft share what is left pro rata. They often accept part payment or delay.
Paid before ordinary shareholders but only after all creditors. They may accept a lower nominal value for a higher dividend rate.
Last in line, so they usually carry the biggest loss. In return they keep control and the upside if the company recovers.

manas.q: Which class should bear the largest loss in a reconstruction?

children.note: Each class should get at least as much under the scheme as in a liquidation, or it will vote no.

manas.q: What is the key fairness test for each class?

children.topic: Is the scheme fair and viable?
children.note: Two questions every exam asks: will it work, and is the pain shared fairly?
Use a realistic profit forecast. After interest and preference dividends, profit must give ordinary shareholders a fair return.
Enough cash to pay debts as they fall due. Check the current ratio and that the overdraft is cleared or within limits.
Profit before interest ÷ interest. A cover of about 3 times or more suggests interest can be paid comfortably.

manas.q: How is interest cover calculated?

children.note: Work out what each class gets if the company is wound up today, then compare with income and capital under the scheme.
See what percentage of the ordinary shares each class holds after. Lenders who take shares gain a say and a share of future profits.
A class moving to riskier securities (debt to shares) should get a higher expected return.
Duma Ltd, a Thika maker of plastic water tanks, is in trouble. All figures in KES million; ignore tax.

Assets: goodwill 40, PPE 380, inventory 150, receivables 130 = 700. Equity and liabilities: ordinary shares (50m × KES 10) 500, 8% preference 100, losses (220), 10% debentures 150, payables 110, overdraft 60 = 700.
Three years of preference dividends (KES 24m) are unpaid. The overdraft is at its limit and the bank wants its money.
The plan agreed with each class, step by step.
Each KES 10 share becomes KES 2: reduction 50m × 8 = 400. They may buy 40m new KES 2 shares for cash (rights issue) = 80.
8% KES 10 shares become 10% KES 8 shares: 100 → 80. Arrears are cancelled in exchange for 2m ordinary KES 2 shares = 4.
Old 10% debentures 150 swapped for 12% debentures 120 plus 10m ordinary KES 2 shares (20). They give up 10.
Losses 220, goodwill 40, PPE down 100 (to 280), inventory down 30 (to 120), receivables down 10 (to 120): total 400.
Rights issue cash 80 repays the overdraft 60, leaving cash 20.
Credits: ordinary 400 + preference 20 + debentures 10 = 430. Debits: write-offs 400 + shares for arrears 4 = 404. Balance 26 goes to capital reserve. 404 + 26 = 430.
Dr Ordinary share capital 400 / Cr Reconstruction 400. Dr 8% Preference 100 / Cr 10% Preference 80, Cr Reconstruction 20.
Dr Reconstruction 4 / Cr Ordinary share capital 4. Dr 10% Debentures 150 / Cr 12% Debentures 120, Cr Ordinary share capital 20, Cr Reconstruction 10.
Dr Reconstruction 400 / Cr Retained losses 220, Cr Goodwill 40, Cr PPE 100, Cr Inventory 30, Cr Receivables 10.
Dr Cash 80 / Cr Ordinary share capital 80. Dr Overdraft 60 / Cr Cash 60. Dr Reconstruction 26 / Cr Capital reserve 26.

Assets: PPE 280, inventory 120, receivables 120, cash 20 = 540. Equity and liabilities: ordinary shares (102m × KES 2) 204, 10% preference 80, capital reserve 26, 12% debentures 120, payables 110 = 540.
Old 100 + preference arrears 4 + debenture holders 20 + rights issue 80 = 204, i.e. 50m + 2m + 10m + 40m = 102m shares.
PPE sells for 160, inventory 60, receivables 90; costs 15.
Secured on PPE: paid 150 in full from 160. Surplus 10 goes to the general pool.
Pool 10 + 60 + 90 − 15 = 145. Owed 110 + 60 = 170. They get 145 ÷ 170 = about 85 cents per shilling: payables 93.8, bank 51.2.
Nothing is left: preference and ordinary shareholders get zero.

Liquidation: 0. Scheme: dividend 8 a year plus 2% of ordinary earnings (0.9).
Liquidation: 0. Scheme: if they take up the rights they own 90 of 102m shares (88%) and about 42.0 of the 47.6.

Mpya issues 30m KES 10 shares (300) and 12% debentures (120) = 420. No goodwill arises.
Dr Assets 500 / Cr Payables 80, Cr Share capital 300, Cr Debentures 120. Debits 500 = credits 500.
If Mpya gives 450 for net assets of 420, the extra 30 is goodwill (IFRS 3).
Changing who owns whom inside a group, often before a sale, listing or rescue. Links to Topic 1, complex groups.
A new parent swaps its shares for all the shares of the old parent. The owners and the business do not change.

manas.q: What is a new holding company reorganisation?

children.topic: Moving a subsidiary inside the group
children.note: A subsidiary is sold or transferred to another group company, e.g. moving it under a regional parent in Kampala.
A group splits a business off and gives its shares directly to the shareholders. Two separate companies result.
IFRS 3 does not cover combinations of companies under the same control. Many groups use book values (predecessor accounting) and create no new goodwill.

manas.q: Does IFRS 3 apply to combinations under common control?

children.note: In the group accounts an internal transfer usually has no effect. In each company's own accounts, the investment and any gain must still be recorded.
Where marks are usually lost.
Undeclared preference dividends are not in the books. Only the shares or cash given for them go through the scheme.
Writing off losses but not bad stock or debts gives an 'after' balance sheet that is still too high.
A scheme where lenders lose more than ordinary shareholders breaks the order of rights. Examiners want you to point this out.
Fairness means nothing without the liquidation comparison for every class.
Writing off losses does not pay bills. Check the plan brings in enough cash to clear urgent debts.
Add both sides before moving on. A difference usually means a missed journal.
Try each one, then open the steps.
Shares are cut to KES 10 to wipe out losses. Find the capital reserve.
Reduction 20m × 10 = KES 200m. Less losses 150m = KES 50m credit to capital reserve. Dr Share capital 200 / Cr Retained losses 150, Cr Capital reserve 50.

children.topic: Q2: what do unsecured creditors get?
children.note: Assets realise KES 300m; costs 20m. A secured loan of 120m is backed by land that sells for 100m. Other unsecured debts 200m.
Secured lender takes 100 from the land; the other 20 joins the unsecured debts: 200 + 20 = 220.
Pool = 300 − 100 − 20 = 180. Payout 180 ÷ 220 = about 82 cents per shilling.

nodeData.note: How to put a fair price on a whole business or its shares. You will meet asset methods, earnings methods, dividend and cash flow methods, and the practical problems of valuing a small unquoted Kenyan company.

children.note: Start here: who needs a value, and why there is never one single right answer.
Value is your estimate of what the business is worth. Price is what a buyer and seller finally agree. A valuation gives a range to negotiate within.

manas.q: What is the difference between value and price in a business sale?

children.note: A buyer wants the most it should pay; a seller wants the least it should accept. Both sides value the target before talks start.
Before a company floats on the Nairobi Securities Exchange, advisers value it to set the offer price for the shares.
Settling a partner leaving, sharing an estate among heirs, giving shares to staff, using shares as loan security, or a court dispute.
You already know cost of capital, NPV and discounting. Most valuation methods here reuse those tools: value is future benefits brought back to today.
Buying over 50% gives control of dividends and strategy, so it is worth more per share. A small minority stake is worth less per share.

manas.q: Why is a controlling stake usually worth more per share than a minority stake?

children.note: Value the business by what it owns minus what it owes (net assets). Simple, and a useful floor value.
Value of equity = total assets − all liabilities (including any preference shares). Divide by ordinary shares for value per share.

manas.q: What is the basic asset-based valuation formula?

children.note: Uses the figures in the statement of financial position. Easy, but book figures are historical cost, so they can be far from today's worth.

manas.q: What is the main weakness of a book value valuation?

children.note: What the assets would sell for if the business closed, less selling and closure costs, less liabilities. Gives a break-up (minimum) value.

manas.q: What does a net realisable value valuation tell a seller?

children.note: What it would cost to buy the same assets new today, less liabilities. Shows the most a buyer should pay to build a copy instead.

manas.q: Why is replacement cost a ceiling for a buyer?

children.note: Asset-heavy firms (property, investment companies), a business being closed, or as a minimum price in talks.
It ignores future profits and things not on the balance sheet, like staff skills, brand and customer lists (intangibles).
Value the business by the profit it makes, multiplied by a market rate. Very common in practice.
Value = earnings × a suitable P/E ratio. Per share: EPS × P/E. The P/E is how many years of profit buyers will pay for.

manas.q: What is the formula for a P/E ratio valuation?

children.note: Use sustainable (maintainable) future profit after tax. Take out one-off items and adjust owner salaries to market rates.
Usually from a similar listed company or the sector average on the NSE. Then adjust it for differences (see Practical issues).
Earnings yield is EPS ÷ share price, the flip side of P/E. Value = earnings ÷ earnings yield.

manas.q: How do you value a business using the earnings yield?

children.note: Earnings yield = 1 ÷ P/E. A P/E of 8 equals an earnings yield of 12.5%.

manas.q: What is the link between P/E ratio and earnings yield?

children.note: Investors expect strong growth or see low risk. A low P/E suggests low growth, high risk, or an undervalued share.
Value a share as today's value of all future dividends, discounted at the cost of equity (ke). Best for minority stakes.
If the dividend never changes: P0 = D ÷ ke. It is a perpetuity, like you met in CA22.

manas.q: What is the DVM formula when dividends are constant?

children.note: If dividends grow at g each year forever: P0 = D0 × (1 + g) ÷ (ke − g). Note the top line is NEXT year's dividend, D1.

manas.q: What is the Gordon growth (dividend growth) model formula?

children.note: g = (latest dividend ÷ oldest dividend)^(1/n) − 1, where n is the number of years of growth between them.

manas.q: How do you estimate g from past dividends?

children.note: g = return on reinvested funds (r) × share of earnings retained (b). Keep 40% and earn 15% on it: g = 0.15 × 0.4 = 6%.

manas.q: What is Gordon's formula for estimating growth?

children.note: The model gives an ex-div value. If the share is cum-div (dividend about to be paid), add the dividend due.
Only works if g is less than ke. Hard to use for firms paying no dividend, and tiny changes in g swing the value a lot.
Value the business as today's value of the cash it will free up in future. The most complete method, and the exam favourite.
Cash left for ALL investors (lenders and shareholders): EBIT × (1 − tax) + depreciation − capital spending − increase in working capital.

manas.q: What is the formula for free cash flow to the firm (FCFF)?

children.note: Cash left for shareholders only: FCFF − interest × (1 − tax) + new borrowing − loan repayments.

manas.q: How do you get from FCFF to FCFE?

children.note: Discount FCFF at WACC to get the whole firm's value. Discount FCFE at ke to get equity value directly. Never mix them.

manas.q: Which rate discounts FCFF and which discounts FCFE?

children.note: After the forecast years, assume steady growth forever: TV at year n = FCF(n) × (1 + g) ÷ (WACC − g). Then discount it back n years.

manas.q: How is terminal value calculated in a DCF valuation?

children.note: FCFF at WACC gives enterprise value. Subtract the market value of debt to get equity value, then divide by number of shares.

manas.q: How do you get from enterprise value to equity value?

children.note: Strong: based on cash and the time value of money. Weak: long forecasts are guesses, and terminal value is often most of the answer.
Two pieces you often need inside a bigger valuation: what the debt is worth, and what the invisible assets are worth.
A bond is worth today's value of its interest and repayment, discounted at what lenders now require (kd, pre-tax).

manas.q: How do you find the market value of a bond?

children.note: Never repaid, so it is a perpetuity: value = annual interest ÷ kd.

manas.q: What is the value of irredeemable debt?

children.note: Value = interest × annuity factor for the years left + redemption amount × discount factor for the final year.
Assets you cannot touch: brand, customer lists, licences, patents, skilled staff. Often worth more than the buildings.
Find profit above what the tangible assets would normally earn, take off tax, then treat that extra profit as a perpetuity at the cost of capital.

manas.q: What are the steps of the calculated intangible value (CIV) method?

children.note: IAS 38 Intangible Assets only lets most self-built intangibles onto the balance sheet in narrow cases, so asset methods tend to miss them.
Illustrative numbers in KES. Each answer has been checked. Where tax is needed, assume tax at 30% for illustration.

nodeData.note: A merger or acquisition joins two businesses under one owner. This topic shows why firms do it, how to pay for a target, how to work out who gains, how targets defend themselves and who must approve deals in Kenya.

children.topic: What M&A is and why it matters
children.note: Start here: the words, the kinds of deal and why accountants care.
In a merger two firms agree to join as one. In an acquisition (takeover) one firm, the bidder, buys control of another, the target.

manas.q: What is the difference between a merger and an acquisition?

children.note: A friendly bid has the support of the target's board. A hostile bid goes straight to the target's shareholders against the board's wishes.

manas.q: What makes a takeover bid hostile?

children.note: Two firms in the same line of business join, e.g. two supermarket chains. Main aims: bigger market share and lower costs.

manas.q: What is a horizontal merger?

children.note: A firm buys a supplier (backwards) or a customer (forwards), e.g. a tea packer buying a tea factory. It secures supply or sales.

manas.q: What is a vertical merger?

children.note: Firms in unrelated businesses join, e.g. a bank buying a hotel. The usual reason is spreading risk, which shareholders can often do more cheaply themselves.

manas.q: What is a conglomerate merger?

children.topic: Recap from topic 1: valuing a business
children.note: You already know asset, earnings (P/E) and cash-flow (DCF) valuations. M&A uses them to set a price range for the target.
Deals are large and hard to undo. Paying too much destroys the bidder shareholders' wealth, so the numbers and the plan must be right.
The main reason to buy is that the two firms are worth more together than apart. That extra value is called synergy.
Synergy is the extra value from combining: value of the combined firm minus the values of the two firms on their own.

manas.q: How do you measure synergy in a merger?

children.note: More sales together: selling each other's products, wider branch network, stronger brand. These are the hardest to achieve.
Lower costs together: one head office, bulk buying, shared IT, closing duplicate branches. These are the easiest to predict.
Cheaper borrowing, using spare cash or unused tax losses, or a more stable combined cash flow.
Faster growth than building from scratch, buying skills or technology, entering a new market or country, and buying an undervalued firm.
Managers may buy to run a bigger empire or to boost EPS through bootstrapping. These do not create real value for shareholders.

manas.q: Name two reasons for a takeover that do not create value for shareholders.

children.note: Many deals never deliver the promised gains. Knowing why helps you test a deal before signing.
Bidders get excited in a contest and pay a premium bigger than the synergy. All the gain then goes to the target's shareholders.

manas.q: What is the most common financial reason acquisitions fail?

children.note: Forecast savings are too hopeful, take longer or cost more to achieve than planned.
Staff from two firms work in different ways. Key people leave and morale drops.
The bidder did not check the target well and finds hidden debts, lawsuits or weak systems after buying.
No clear plan for joining systems, people and customers after the deal, so the business drifts.
The bidder must choose what to give the target shareholders. Each method shares risk and gains differently.
Target shareholders get cash. It is simple and certain for them, but the bidder must have or borrow the money.

manas.q: What are the main pros and cons of a cash offer?

children.note: Target shareholders get new bidder shares. No cash is needed, but bidder holders' ownership is diluted and target holders share future risk.

manas.q: What is a share-for-share exchange?

children.note: Part cash, part shares. It balances the bidder's cash needs with what target holders want.
Part of the price is paid later only if the target hits agreed targets, e.g. profit. It protects the bidder and keeps the sellers motivated.

manas.q: What is an earn-out?

children.note: Bidder pays KES 300m now plus KES 100m in year 2 if the target's profit reaches KES 50m. Most it can pay: 300 + 100 = KES 400m.
Number of bidder shares given for each target share, e.g. 3 for 4 = 0.75. New shares issued = target shares x ratio.

manas.q: How do you work out the number of new shares issued in a share exchange?

children.note: Lowest price: the target's value on its own. Highest price: that value plus the full synergy. The deal sits between the two.

manas.q: What are the minimum and maximum prices in a takeover negotiation?

children.note: After a share deal, work out the new EPS, the new share price and how much each group of shareholders gained.
Bidder earnings + target earnings + any extra earnings from synergy.

manas.q: How do you find the combined earnings after a merger?

children.note: Combined earnings divided by (bidder's old shares + new shares issued).

manas.q: What is the formula for post-merger EPS?

children.note: Combined value (combined earnings x expected P/E) divided by total shares after the deal.

manas.q: How do you estimate the post-merger share price?

children.note: Bidder gain = old shares x new price minus old value. Target gain = value received minus old value. The two gains add up to the synergy.

manas.q: How do the gains to each set of shareholders relate to the synergy?

children.note: When a high P/E firm buys a low P/E firm with shares, EPS rises even with no synergy. If the market keeps the high P/E, the price rises too.

manas.q: What is bootstrapping in mergers?

children.note: No new profit is made. A sensible market will use a weighted P/E for the combined firm, so the price stays the same.
Illustrative KES figures. Amani Ltd (bidder) buys Baraka Ltd (target). All amounts in KES millions unless shown.
Amani: earnings 120, 60m shares, EPS 2.00, P/E 15, price KES 30, value 1,800. Baraka: earnings 40, 20m shares, EPS 2.00, P/E 10, price KES 20, value 400.
Extra earnings of 10 a year. Combined earnings 120 + 40 + 10 = 170. Expected P/E 14, so combined value 170 x 14 = 2,380. Synergy = 2,380 - 1,800 - 400 = 180.
Amani offers 3 new shares for every 4 Baraka shares (ratio 0.75). At KES 30 that is KES 22.50 per Baraka share, a 12.5% premium on KES 20.
New shares = 20m x 0.75 = 15m. Total shares 60m + 15m = 75m. Post-merger EPS = 170 / 75 = KES 2.27, up from KES 2.00.
Amani holders: 60m x 31.73 = 1,904, gain 104. Baraka holders: 15m x 31.73 = 476, gain 76. Total 104 + 76 = 180 = synergy.
Cash paid = 20m x 24 = 480. Amani's value after paying: 2,380 - 480 = 1,900, so price = 1,900 / 60m = KES 31.67.
Amani gain = 1,900 - 1,800 = 100. Baraka gain = 480 - 400 = 80. Total 180 = synergy.
For each Baraka share: KES 10 cash plus 0.5 Amani share. Cash 200; new shares 10m; value left 2,380 - 200 = 2,180 over 70m shares = KES 31.14.
Amani: 60m x 31.14 = 1,868.6, gain 68.6. Baraka: 200 + 10m x 31.14 = 511.4, gain 111.4. Total 180 = synergy.
Amani holders lose if the price falls below KES 30: 2,380 / 30 = 79.33m shares, so at most 19.33m new shares (ratio 0.97).
Baraka holders need value of at least 400: new shares n where 2,380n / (60 + n) = 400, so n = 12.12m (ratio 0.61).
Baraka value 400 + full synergy 180 = 580, or KES 29 per share. Above that Amani holders lose.
Juu Ltd: earnings 60, 30m shares, EPS 2.00, price 30 (P/E 15). Chini Ltd: earnings 20, 10m shares, price 15 (P/E 7.5), value 150. No synergy.
Shares issued at market: 150 / 30 = 5m. New EPS = 80 / 35m = KES 2.29, up 14.3%, with no new profit.
If P/E stays 15: 2.29 x 15 = KES 34.29 (an illusion). Weighted P/E = 1,050 / 80 = 13.125, giving 2.29 x 13.125 = KES 30, no change.
A target board that thinks a bid is too low or harmful can fight it, but must act in the shareholders' interest, not to protect jobs.
Publish better profit forecasts, revalue assets and argue the bid undervalues the firm.
The target finds a friendlier bidder to make a better offer.

manas.q: What is a white knight defence?

children.note: A plan that makes the target costly to take over, e.g. letting existing holders buy cheap new shares if a bidder crosses a stake level.

manas.q: What is a poison pill?

children.note: The target sells or promises away its most valuable asset so it is less attractive.
The target turns round and bids for the bidder.
For listed companies, takeover rules usually stop the board taking frustrating action without shareholder approval once a bid is made.
The deal is only the start. Value comes from joining the businesses well.
Name an integration leader, set the first 100 days' tasks and the synergy targets.

In the group accounts the deal is a business combination under IFRS 3: fair value the net assets and record goodwill.
Several bodies may need to approve a deal. Check each one's website for the current rules before you start.

manas.q: Which Kenyan body controls mergers under the Competition Act?

children.note: If a deal counts as a merger under the Act, check with CAK whether it must be notified and approved before completion. See cak.go.ke for current rules.

Easy marks are lost here. Check these before you hand in.
Combined earnings must include the extra earnings from synergy, not just the two profits added.
Divide by old bidder shares plus the new shares issued, not the old shares alone.
3 bidder shares for 4 target shares means new shares = target shares x 3/4, not x 4/3.
Bidder gain plus target gain must equal the synergy. If not, recheck the price.
Higher EPS from bootstrapping is not a gain. Ask whether the market will keep the higher P/E.
In a cash deal, take the cash paid off the combined value before working out the bidder's price.
Try each one, then open the steps. Figures in KES millions.

No. Earnings are just spread over shares bought cheaply. With a weighted P/E the share price is unchanged.

maps.title: CA33 · 3. Managing currency and interest-rate risk

nodeData.note: How Kenyan businesses protect themselves when exchange rates or interest rates move. You will learn the kinds of exposure, cheap internal fixes, bank hedges for currency and interest rates, and the parity theories behind forward rates.

children.note: Start here: why a change in the shilling or in interest rates can hurt a Kenyan business.
The risk that the exchange rate moves before you pay or get paid, so you end up with fewer shillings, or pay more shillings, than you planned (foreign exchange risk).

manas.q: What is foreign exchange (currency) risk?

children.note: The risk that interest rates move and raise what you pay on loans, or cut what you earn on deposits, or change the value of fixed-rate items.

manas.q: What is interest-rate risk?

children.note: Many Kenyan firms import fuel, machines and medicines in USD, and export tea, flowers and coffee for EUR, GBP or USD. Many bank loans are on floating rates.
Hedging means fixing or limiting a future cost or income now, so a bad move in rates does not hurt you. You often give up some gain from a good move.

manas.q: What does it mean to hedge a risk?

children.note: Topic 1 (valuing a business) and Topic 2 (mergers and acquisitions) used cash flows and discount rates. Here we protect those cash flows. CA32 Topic 2 covered how foreign currency is recorded in the books (IAS 21).

children.topic: All rates here are made up
children.note: Every exchange and interest rate in this map is an example only (illustrative rate, not today's). Always get live quotes from your bank or the Central Bank of Kenya website.
Exposure means how much of your money is open to a rate move. There are three kinds.
Risk on a deal already agreed in a foreign currency, such as an unpaid USD invoice. The shilling amount changes until the day of payment.

manas.q: What is transaction exposure?

children.note: Risk that the group's balance sheet changes when a foreign subsidiary's accounts are turned into KES. It is an accounting effect; no cash moves (IAS 21 puts the difference in other comprehensive income).

manas.q: What is translation (accounting) exposure?

children.note: Risk that long-term rate moves change the value of the whole business, for example a strong shilling making Kenyan tea dearer than Sri Lankan tea abroad.

manas.q: What is economic exposure?

children.note: Forwards, money market hedges, futures and options mainly deal with transaction exposure. Economic exposure needs business choices, like where to buy and sell.
A Nairobi pharmacy chain owes a supplier USD 200,000 in 3 months. If the shilling weakens, the bill in KES goes up. That is transaction exposure.
A Naivasha flower farm will receive EUR 500,000 in 6 months. If the shilling strengthens, it gets fewer shillings. That is transaction exposure too.
Before paying a bank, see what you can fix yourself. These methods cost little or nothing.
Ask the buyer or supplier to use shillings. The risk then moves to the other side. Works only if they agree.

manas.q: How does invoicing in your home currency reduce risk?

children.note: Paying early. An importer who expects the shilling to fall pays the USD bill now, before it costs more.

manas.q: What is leading?

children.note: Paying late. If you expect the foreign currency to get cheaper, delay payment (within the credit terms).
Group companies cancel what they owe each other and pay only the net balance. Example: a Kenyan parent and its Uganda and Tanzania subsidiaries settle once a month.

manas.q: What is netting?

children.note: Match foreign income with foreign costs in the same currency. A flower exporter earning EUR can borrow in EUR and repay the loan with EUR sales.

manas.q: What is matching?

children.note: Tools you buy from a bank or exchange to fix or limit the rate.
A deal with a bank today to buy or sell a set amount of currency on a set future date at a rate fixed today. Binding on both sides.

manas.q: What is a forward exchange contract?

children.note: Banks quote two rates, e.g. KES/USD 129.20–129.80 (illustrative rate, not today's). The bank sells USD to you at the higher rate and buys USD from you at the lower one.
Use borrowing and deposits to fix the rate today. Payable: buy the currency now and deposit it until due. Receivable: borrow the currency now and convert it at spot.

manas.q: What is a money market hedge?

children.note: Like a forward, but a standard contract traded on an exchange, with a margin account settled daily. Sizes are fixed (e.g. EUR 125,000 per CME euro contract), so hedges may not fit exactly.

manas.q: How do currency futures differ from forwards?

children.note: The right, not the duty, to buy (call) or sell (put) currency at a set rate (strike). You pay a premium upfront. Protects against bad moves but keeps good ones.

manas.q: What is a currency option?

children.note: Two parties swap principal in two currencies at the start, pay each other's interest, then swap the principal back at the end. Used for long-term foreign loans.

manas.q: What is a currency swap?

children.note: Compare the KES cost or receipt of each method. Pick the best cash result, then think about flexibility, premium cost and counterparty risk.
Two theories explain how exchange rates link to interest and inflation. They guide forecasts; real rates also swing with trade, debt and politics.
The forward rate reflects the interest gap. Forward = spot × (1 + home rate) ÷ (1 + foreign rate), with both rates for the same period. The higher-rate currency is weaker in the forward.

manas.q: What is the interest rate parity formula?

children.note: Exchange rates move to keep prices equal. Expected rate = spot × (1 + home inflation) ÷ (1 + foreign inflation).

manas.q: What is the purchasing power parity formula?

children.note: Interest rate gaps reflect inflation gaps, so the high-interest currency is expected to weaken over time.
Most Kenyan firms borrow from banks. Here is how to manage the rate on those loans.
Fixed rate: same rate for the loan life. Floating rate: moves with a reference rate plus a margin. Floating is cheaper when rates fall, dearer when they rise.

manas.q: What is the difference between fixed and floating interest?

children.note: Compare assets and liabilities whose rates reset in the same period. If more liabilities reset than assets, a rate rise cuts profit (a negative gap).

manas.q: What is gap exposure?

children.note: A deal fixing the interest rate on a future loan or deposit period. Only the rate difference is settled in cash; the loan itself is separate.

manas.q: What is a forward rate agreement (FRA)?

children.note: A 3v9 FRA starts in 3 months and ends in 9 months, so it covers a 6-month period.
Exchange-traded contracts priced at 100 minus the rate. A borrower fearing a rise SELLS futures; if rates rise, the price falls and the futures gain covers the extra interest.

manas.q: How is an interest rate future priced, and what does a borrower do?

children.note: An option that sets a top rate on a floating loan. You pay a premium; if rates go above the cap, the seller pays you the difference.

manas.q: What is an interest rate cap?

children.note: An option that sets a bottom rate, used by depositors and lenders. It pays out if rates fall below the floor.
Buy a cap and sell a floor together. The floor premium you earn cuts the cap cost, but you lose gains below the floor.

manas.q: What is an interest rate collar?

children.note: Two parties swap interest payments on the same notional amount, usually fixed for floating. The loans stay with each party; only interest flows are swapped.

manas.q: What is an interest rate swap?

children.note: A swap pays off when one party borrows relatively cheaper in fixed and the other in floating. The gain is the difference between the two rate gaps.
Real numbers in KES. All rates are illustrative, not today's. Every figure is checked.
A Nairobi importer pays USD 200,000 in 3 months. Rates (illustrative rate, not today's): spot KES/USD 129.20–129.80; 3-month forward 132.90 (offer); USD deposit 4% a year; KES borrowing 14% a year.
3-month USD rate = 4% ÷ 4 = 1%. Deposit 200,000 ÷ 1.01 = USD 198,019.80 now; it grows to USD 200,000.
198,019.80 × 129.80 (bank sells USD) = KES 25,702,970.30, borrowed in KES.
Forward 26,580,000 vs MMH 26,602,574.26. The forward is cheaper by KES 22,574.26, so use the forward.

A Naivasha flower farm receives EUR 500,000 in 6 months. Rates (illustrative rate, not today's): spot KES/EUR 150.00 (bank buys); 6-month forward 154.00 (bank buys); EUR borrowing 4% a year; KES deposit 10% a year.
6-month EUR rate = 2%. Borrow 500,000 ÷ 1.02 = EUR 490,196.08. The EUR 500,000 receipt repays it with interest.
MMH 77,205,882.35 vs forward 77,000,000. The MMH gives KES 205,882.35 more, so use it here.
Spot KES/USD 130.00. Kenya: interest 12%, inflation 6%. US: interest 4%, inflation 2% (illustrative rate, not today's).
Both say the shilling should weaken against the USD, because Kenyan rates and inflation are higher.
The importer in Example 1 instead buys a call on USD 200,000 at strike 132.00, premium KES 1.00 per USD (KES 200,000) (illustrative rate, not today's). Premium interest is ignored.
Let it lapse and buy at spot: 200,000 × 128.00 = 25,600,000 + premium 200,000 = KES 25,800,000.

children.topic: Example 5: FRA on a bank loan
children.note: A firm will borrow KES 100m in 3 months for 6 months at the reference rate + 2%. It buys a 3v9 FRA at 12% (illustrative rate, not today's).
Bank pays the firm (14% − 12%) × 100m × 6/12 = KES 1,000,000. Loan interest 16% × 100m × 6/12 = 8,000,000. Net cost KES 7,000,000.
Either way the cost is 7,000,000 on 100m for half a year = 14% a year: the FRA 12% plus the 2% margin.
A SACCO has KES 80m of loans and KES 120m of deposits resetting within 3 months. Gap = 80m − 120m = negative KES 40m. A 1% rise for a year cuts profit by 40m × 1% = KES 400,000.

children.topic: Example 7: collar on a floating loan
children.note: KES 100m floating loan. Buy a cap at 13% (premium 0.5%) and sell a floor at 10% (premium earned 0.3%): net premium 0.2% (illustrative rate, not today's).
Cap pays the excess. Cost = 13% + 0.2% = 13.2%, i.e. KES 13.2m a year.
The floor holds you at 10%. Cost = 10% + 0.2% = 10.2%, i.e. KES 10.2m a year.
A tea exporter (A) can borrow fixed 11% or floating base + 1%. A smaller firm (B) pays fixed 13% or base + 2% (illustrative rate, not today's). A wants floating, B wants fixed. No bank fee.
Gap in fixed 2%, gap in floating 1%. Saving = 2% − 1% = 1%, split 0.5% each.
A borrows fixed at 11%. B borrows floating at base + 2%. Then they swap.
B pays A a fixed 10.5%. A pays B the base rate.
Pays 11% + base, gets 10.5% = base + 0.5%. Saves 0.5% vs base + 1%.
Pays base + 2% + 10.5%, gets base = 12.5% fixed. Saves 0.5% vs 13%. Total 0.5% + 0.5% = 1%.
On KES 200m each, 0.5% = KES 1,000,000 a year saved by each party.
